lessons.title: Skill, Ability and the Classification of Skills
lessons.description: Skill versus ability, the four classification continuums and sporting examples.
lessons.content_html:
Skill and Ability — Two Different Things

In everyday conversation, people use “skill” and “ability” as if they mean the same thing. In physical education, they do not. Skill is something you develop through practice. It is learned, purposeful and can be refined over time. A novice swimmer performing front crawl for the first time is displaying very little skill; an Olympic swimmer performing the same stroke is highly skilled because years of deliberate practice have made the action consistent, efficient and well-controlled.

Ability, by contrast, is something you are born with. It is a stable, largely unchangeable trait that sets the upper limit of what you can potentially achieve. Abilities include things like reaction time, balance, limb coordination and explosive power. You cannot teach someone better reaction time the way you can teach them better technique — genetic endowment places a ceiling on these qualities. A sprinter like Dina Asher-Smith had natural fast-twitch muscle fibre capacity (an ability) long before she had refined sprint technique (a skill). The skill was developed through coaching; the ability was always there.

Key Fact

Skill is learned and can be improved through practice. Ability is innate (natural, inherited) and sets the performer’s potential ceiling. A talented young gymnast may have excellent natural balance (ability) but still needs years of practice to execute a beam routine without error (skill).

The Four Classification Continuums

Skills are not simply “good” or “bad” — they vary across four dimensions. Each dimension is best understood as a continuum rather than a binary choice, because most skills fall somewhere between the two extremes. Examiners expect you to place a skill on the continuum and justify your choice, not just label it.

1. Basic — Complex

A basic skill demands very little from the performer in terms of decision-making or perceptual processing. Walking, running in a straight line, or a simple underarm throw all sit towards the basic end. A complex skill, at the other end, involves many sub-routines to be coordinated simultaneously, a wide range of possible responses, and heavy attentional demands. A tennis serve — which requires ball toss timing, racket path, weight transfer, wrist snap and ball placement all to be synchronised — sits towards the complex end. A basketball lay-up sits between the two: it has a set pattern (making it less random) but requires coordination of running, jumping and release angle (making it more demanding than a simple catch).

2. Open — Closed

This is one of the most frequently confused continuums. Open and closed refer to the predictability of the environment, not to whether the skill is simple or difficult. An open skill takes place in an unstable environment. A football pass under pressure from a defender is an open skill because the environment — positions of teammates, defenders, ball bounce — changes from moment to moment and the performer must constantly adapt. In contrast, a closed skill takes place in a stable environment. A gymnast performing a floor routine performs each move in a predictable, unchanging space; a swimmer at the start of a race dives into the same lane each time. Because the environment is stable, the movement pattern can be pre-planned and repeated identically.

Many students write that a skill is “open because it is difficult” or “closed because it is simple” — this is wrong and will lose marks. A highly complex gymnastics routine is a closed skill because the environment is predictable. A simple one-touch pass in football is an open skill because defenders and teammates are moving and the performer must react to them. Always base your answer on whether the environment is changing and unpredictable (open) or stable and predictable (closed).

3. Self-Paced — Externally Paced

This continuum refers to who controls the timing of the skill. In a self-paced skill, the performer chooses when to start and how fast to execute. A golfer selecting their moment to drive, a gymnast deciding when to begin her vault run-up, or a footballer taking a penalty all control their own timing. In an externally paced skill, external factors dictate when the performer must respond. A cricket batsman facing a delivery must time their shot to the ball, not to their own preference. A hockey player receiving a pass must react to the arriving ball. The more an athlete must react to something outside their control, the further towards the externally paced end the skill sits.

4. Gross — Fine

The gross — fine continuum is about the muscles involved and the precision required. A gross skill uses large muscle groups: running, jumping, throwing, swimming. The movements are powerful and whole-body. A fine skill requires delicate coordination of small muscle groups — the hands, fingers and wrists. A snooker player potting a ball, an archer releasing the bowstring with a relaxed grip, or a dart player aiming at the treble 20 all involve fine skills. Note that fine skills do not have to be low effort — a surgeon’s instrument control is fine but intense. Fine skills also typically demand precision that gross skills do not.

Key Fact

The four continuums — basic/complex, open/closed, self-paced/externally paced, gross/fine — allow you to describe and compare ANY skill systematically. Most skills sit between the extremes. A cricket batting stroke, for example, is towards the complex, open, externally paced and gross end of each continuum.

A tennis serve can be placed on all four continuums:

Basic — Complex: Towards the complex end. The serve involves multiple sub-routines — ball toss, stance, backswing, contact point, follow-through — all of which must be coordinated precisely.

Open — Closed: Towards the closed end when serving first. The server controls the environment: the court is always the same dimensions, the ball is stationary in their hand, and the serve begins when they choose. However, for the returner, receiving a serve is an open skill because the ball direction and speed are unpredictable.

Self-Paced — Externally Paced: Self-paced. The server decides exactly when to toss the ball and begin the swing. No external factor dictates their timing.

Gross — Fine: Towards the gross end. The serve uses large muscle groups of the legs, torso, shoulder and arm. However, the final wrist snap and precise contact point add a fine element, placing it slightly towards the middle.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘explain’ and ‘analyse’ questions about skill classification, the most common error is stating a classification without justifying it. A marker will not credit “it is an open skill” alone — you must say why using the continuum definition (e.g. “it is an open skill because the environment is unpredictable — defenders are moving and the performer must adapt continuously”). For a 6-mark analyse question, select at least two of the four continuums, place the skill precisely, and give a sporting example for each. Avoid writing “this skill is open because it is complex” — these are separate continuums and must be justified separately. On multiple-choice and identify questions, re-read the continuum labels carefully: self-paced means the performer controls timing, not that the skill is easy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Skill is learned through practice; ability is innate and sets the performer’s potential ceiling — a key distinction the spec tests with definition questions.
  • Skills are classified on four continuums: basic/complex (decisions and sub-routines), open/closed (predictability of environment), self-paced/externally paced (who controls timing), and gross/fine (muscles used and precision required).
  • Most skills sit between the extremes of each continuum. Always justify your classification using the definition of the continuum, not just the label.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a closed skill?
A) A football player receiving a through pass from a teammate
B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat
C) A hockey player hitting a moving ball past a goalkeeper
D) A basketball player taking a free throw during a fast break
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ability' in the context of sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: ability is an innate / natural / inherited characteristic. 1 mark for development: it is stable and largely unchangeable; it underpins a performer's potential to learn and perform skills (accept: it sets a ceiling on what a performer can achieve). Do not credit definitions that describe ability as learned or practised.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use the four skill classification continuums to analyse a performer's front crawl stroke.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each continuum correctly applied with a brief justification (max 3 continuums credited). Examples: Basic/complex — complex, because it requires simultaneous coordination of arm pull, leg kick, breathing pattern and head position (1). Open/closed — closed, because the pool environment is stable and the performer moves through predictable conditions (1). Self-paced/externally paced — self-paced, because the swimmer decides their own stroke rate and turn timing (1). Gross/fine — gross, because large muscle groups of the arms, shoulders, core and legs produce the movement (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a basketball player taking a free throw is classified differently on the open/closed continuum compared to the same player making a lay-up during open play. Use the definitions of open and closed skills in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a free throw is a closed skill. 1 mark for justification: the environment is stable and predictable; the player stands at the same spot, no defenders can challenge, and the timing is self-controlled. 1 mark for identifying that a lay-up in open play is an open skill (or further towards the open end). 1 mark for justification: the environment is unpredictable; defenders are moving, teammates are repositioning, and the player must adapt their movement and timing to the changing situation.

practice_questions.text: A Year-10 PE teacher is designing classification tasks for two groups: one group will practise hitting a stationary ball on a tee, the other will practise hitting a ball bowled at them by a partner. Analyse how the four continuums differ between these two tasks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses all four continuums, clearly differentiating both tasks on each, with precise definitions and specific justifications rooted in the scenario. Points might include: basic/complex — hitting a stationary ball is more basic (fewer decisions, simpler movement), while hitting a bowled ball is more complex (timing judgement, footwork, range of shots possible); open/closed — stationary ball is closed (environment controlled, ball position fixed), bowled ball is open (ball direction, speed, bounce variable); self-paced/externally paced — tee hit is self-paced (performer starts when ready), bowled ball is externally paced (bowler dictates timing); gross/fine — both are gross skills (large muscle groups driving the shot) but the tee hit may be slightly more fine near the point of contact. Consistent reference to both tasks throughout.

Secure: Correctly analyses at least three continuums, with most justifications accurate. Generally applies to both tasks but may be less precise on one or two.

Developing: Names and partially explains two or three continuums. May label without justifying, or analyse only one task.

Emerging: Names one or two continuums; limited or no justification; may confuse continuum definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old club athlete competes in both archery and rugby union. Evaluate the view that classifying skills on the four continuums helps coaches plan training more effectively than simply labelling skills as 'easy' or 'hard'. Use examples from both sports in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to specific sporting examples from archery and/or rugby, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the four continuums reveal specific training needs — knowing an archery shot is closed, self-paced and fine tells a coach to prioritise consistency of technique and mental routine rather than reaction speed or physical power; classifying a rugby tackle as open, externally paced and gross directs training towards reactive drills and contact conditioning rather than technical precision; using continuums prevents coaches from applying the wrong training prescription, e.g. drilling a rugby player in closed-skill repetition when open-skill adaptability is what match performance demands; continuums allow comparison of a performer's current skill level to the demands of the full game situation. Arguments against or limitations: classifying skills is time-consuming and most coaches work intuitively from experience; the four continuums may oversimplify — many skills shift along continuums depending on context (a tennis serve is closed when initiating but the rally is open); beginners may benefit more from straightforward 'easy/hard' progression than from theoretical classification. Justified conclusion: the four continuums are most useful when planning training progression, especially when designing drills that match real competition demands.

Secure: Two or three points on each side, mostly applied to both sports, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; sporting context present but thin or one-sport only.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application.

lessons.title: Goal Setting and SMART Targets
lessons.description: Performance and outcome goals and how SMART targets improve sporting performance.
lessons.content_html:
Why Goal Setting Matters in Sport

Elite and recreational athletes alike use goal setting to direct effort, maintain motivation and track progress. Without a clearly defined target, training can feel purposeless — athletes may work hard without knowing what they are working towards. Goal setting provides a focus, helps athletes manage anxiety before competition, and gives coaches a framework for structuring training sessions. Psychologists working with performers at all levels recognise two fundamentally different types of goal: performance goals and outcome goals.

Performance Goals

A performance goal focuses on what the individual does, measured against their own previous best. “Run 400 m in under 55 seconds”, “serve 80% of first serves in during my next match” or “complete a set of 12 pull-ups by the end of the month” are all performance goals. Crucially, the performer can influence these outcomes directly through their own effort and technique — no one else’s performance can stop them achieving a personal best. This makes performance goals particularly valuable for motivation: even if you lose the match, you may still have achieved your performance goal, leaving you with a sense of progress and self-efficacy. Research and sporting practice consistently show that performance goals are the more effective type for long-term development.

Outcome Goals

An outcome goal focuses on the result of competition — winning the game, finishing first, or topping the league. The difficulty with outcome goals is that they depend on factors outside the athlete’s control. A club runner may achieve a personal best in a 10 km race and still finish last in a strong field. If winning was the only goal, that race feels like a failure — despite excellent individual performance. For beginners in particular, outcome goals can be demotivating: if winning is unrealistic against more experienced opponents, repeated “failure” can reduce confidence and participation. The spec makes it clear that outcome goals are generally better avoided — or used only alongside performance goals — because they rely on factors the performer cannot control.

Outcome goals are not entirely without value — for highly experienced performers competing at the top of their sport, knowing that the target is to win a final can sharpen focus and intensity. The key is that outcome goals work best when combined with specific performance goals. An elite rower might set an outcome goal (win the national championship) alongside several performance goals (reduce 2,000 m split time to 6:08; improve catch angle consistency). The performance goals provide a daily, controllable target; the outcome goal provides motivating context. For most students and developing performers, however, performance goals should dominate the plan, with outcome goals treated as a background aspiration rather than the main measure of success.

Key Fact

Outcome goals rely on factors outside the performer’s control — the quality of opponents, referee decisions, weather. Beginners should avoid them because: winning may be unrealistic against experienced opponents; repeated “failure” can demotivate; and they shift focus away from technique development onto the scoreboard.

SMART Targets

A goal is only useful if it is well-constructed. The SMART framework provides a checklist for turning vague intentions into actionable targets. SMART stands for: Specific, Measurable, Accepted, Realistic and Time-bound. Note that the AQA specification uses “accepted” — not “achievable” — as the A in SMART.

Breaking Down SMART

Specific: the target must state clearly what is to be achieved. “Get better at swimming” is not specific. “Reduce my 100 m freestyle time from 75 seconds to 70 seconds” is specific. A specific goal focuses training effort on the right area.

Measurable: progress must be trackable using objective data. Times, distances, repetition counts, percentage success rates and scores all provide measurable evidence of progress. Without a measurable element, the performer cannot tell whether they are improving.

Accepted: the target must be agreed upon and “bought into” by both the performer and their coach or support team. If a coach sets a goal without the athlete’s input, the athlete is less likely to be committed to it. When the goal is agreed together, both parties take ownership and work cooperatively toward it.

Realistic: the goal must be achievable given the performer’s current level. Setting a goal that is too easy provides no challenge and little sense of achievement when reached. Setting a goal that is impossible to reach leads to repeated failure and loss of motivation. A realistic goal is stretching but attainable — just beyond what the performer is currently capable of.

Time-bound: every SMART goal needs a deadline. “Improve my press-up maximum to 30 by the end of this half-term” has a time-bound element; “improve my press-ups eventually” does not. A deadline creates urgency, helps coaches plan progressive overload across a training programme, and provides a natural review point.

Key Fact

SMART = Specific, Measurable, Accepted (agreed with coach), Realistic (challenging but achievable), Time-bound (has a deadline). AQA uses “Accepted” — not “Achievable” — as the A. Using “achievable” may still earn the mark in context, but learn the correct term to be safe.

Imagine a 15-year-old club midfielder whose conversion rate from shooting practice is 40%. A SMART target might be:

“Increase my scoring conversion rate in shooting practice sessions from 40% to 55% (specific, measurable) over the next six weeks of training (time-bound). My coach and I have agreed this is achievable if I focus on my first touch before shooting and stay for 30 extra minutes of practice each Friday (realistic, accepted).”

Notice that this is a performance goal (based on the player’s own conversion rate, not on match results), and every element of SMART is present. The accepted element is demonstrated by the coach’s involvement in setting and agreeing to the plan.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On 9-mark evaluate questions about goal setting, a common error is arguing only one side — for example, only criticising outcome goals without acknowledging any merit. To reach the highest band, you must consider both sides and apply your points to a sporting context. Structure each point as: state the idea → develop it → apply to a sporting example (e.g. “outcome goals can demotivate beginners because winning is unrealistic — a new tennis player facing a county-standard opponent may score zero games and feel they have completely failed, reducing their desire to continue”). On 3-mark describe or 4-mark explain questions asking you to describe a SMART target, always include the letter A stands for ‘accepted’ — not ‘achievable’ — as this is the most frequently penalised mistake.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Performance goals (based on personal improvement) are generally more effective than outcome goals (based on results), because performers can directly control their own effort and technique but cannot control opponents or external factors.
  • Beginners should avoid relying on outcome goals — repeated failure when winning is unrealistic can demotivate and reduce participation.
  • SMART targets must be Specific, Measurable, Accepted (agreed with coach), Realistic and Time-bound. The AQA spec uses ‘accepted’ not ‘achievable’ — a crucial detail to learn.

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why beginners are advised to avoid setting outcome goals.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: winning may be unrealistic against more experienced opponents (1); repeated failure can demotivate the performer (1); outcome goals rely on factors outside the performer's control, such as the quality of opponents (1). Do not credit 'outcome goals are bad' without explanation.

practice_questions.text: State two characteristics of a performance goal.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct characteristics: it is based on personal improvement rather than the result (1); it is judged against the performer's own previous standard, not against others (1); the performer can directly influence whether the goal is achieved through their own effort and technique (1). Maximum 2 marks. Do not credit two descriptions of the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a SMART target in physical education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly named and briefly explained element, up to 3 marks. Accept any three of: Specific — the goal is precisely defined (1); Measurable — progress can be tracked using numbers or data (1); Accepted — the goal is agreed between performer and coach (1); Realistic — the goal is challenging but achievable given current ability (1); Time-bound — the goal has a clear deadline (1). Note: mark as 'accepted' for the A — credit 'achievable' only if accompanied by a correct description.

practice_questions.text: A county-level netball player has set the following goal: 'Win the regional cup final next season.' Explain why this goal might not be effective, and suggest how it could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the critique: the goal is an outcome goal / result-dependent (1); the player cannot control other teams' performance, referee decisions or opponent quality (1); if the team does not win, the player may feel they have failed regardless of their personal contribution, reducing motivation (1). Up to 2 marks for the improvement: a suggested performance goal e.g. 'increase interception rate from 4 to 7 per match over the next 10 games' (1); the improvement must demonstrate at least two SMART elements to earn the second mark — e.g. specific and time-bound / measurable and realistic (1).

practice_questions.text: A sports coach argues that outcome goals are always harmful to performance and should never be used. Evaluate this view, using examples from sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on both sides, each applied to a specific sporting example, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support of the coach's view: outcome goals depend on factors outside the performer's control — if a swimmer trains excellently but finishes second because of a stronger competitor, an outcome-only focus feels like failure (apply: club swimmer aiming to win county championship); for beginners, outcome goals are particularly damaging because winning against experienced opponents is unrealistic, leading to repeated demotivation and potential dropout from sport; outcome goals can increase anxiety before competition rather than focusing the performer on their own preparation. Arguments against the coach's view: outcome goals provide motivating direction for elite performers who are competing seriously for titles — knowing the target is the national championship focuses training intensity; outcome goals can be combined effectively with performance goals, so the performer has both a controllable daily target and a longer-term competitive aim; some performers are naturally outcome-oriented and respond well to competition-based targets, using a loss as a stimulus to train harder. Conclusion: outcome goals should generally be avoided or used only alongside performance goals, especially for beginners; for elite performers, a blend is most effective.

Secure: Two or three well-developed points on each side, mostly applied to sporting examples, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; sporting context thin or inconsistent.

Emerging: One-sided response or very basic points; little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Write a SMART target for a 16-year-old county-level javelin thrower who currently throws an average of 28 metres and wants to improve before the county championships in eight weeks.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific and measurable element (e.g. 'throw an average of 32 metres in the county championships' — this includes a specific distance and the named event). 1 mark for accepted/realistic element: the target is agreed with the coach and is achievable given 8 weeks of training — an increase of 4 m is challenging but realistic for a county-level athlete (1). 1 mark for time-bound element: 'within 8 weeks / before the county championships' is explicit and measurable (1). Accept alternative distances or timelines provided they are internally consistent and justified.

lessons.title: Information Processing in Sport
lessons.description: Input, decision making, output and feedback applied to sport and skill learning.
lessons.content_html:
Why Performers Need to Process Information

Every movement in sport begins with the brain receiving information from the environment and deciding how to respond. A netball player catching a pass, a goalkeeper preparing for a penalty, a sprinter reacting to the gun — all of them are processing information before they act. Sports psychologists use the information processing model to describe this sequence. Understanding the model helps coaches identify where a performer is breaking down — are they missing key cues (input problem), making wrong choices (decision making problem), or executing the wrong movement (output problem)?

Stage 1 — Input

The input stage is where the performer gathers information from the display — everything around them that could be relevant. The senses provide raw data: eyes track the position of the ball and defenders, ears pick up shouts from teammates, proprioceptors in muscles and joints provide information about body position and balance. However, the display contains far more information than the brain can fully process at once. This is where selective attention becomes critical. Selective attention is the performer’s ability to focus on relevant stimuli and filter out distractions. An experienced midfielder reading the game attends to teammates’ runs and opponents’ positions while ignoring crowd noise and irrelevant movement. A novice player, overwhelmed by the display, struggles to attend selectively — they look at the ball rather than scanning the field, or freeze under pressure because too many stimuli compete for attention. Coaching and practice improve selective attention by teaching performers which cues are significant.

Key Fact

The four stages of the information processing model are: Input (gathering information via the senses from the display) → Decision Making (selecting the appropriate response using memory) → Output (sending instructions to muscles to produce movement) → Feedback (receiving information about the outcome of the movement). The cycle then repeats.

Stage 2 — Decision Making

Once relevant information has been attended to, the performer must decide what to do. Decision making draws on two types of memory. Short-term memory (also called working memory) holds the immediate situation: the current positions of players, the recent pattern of play, the score. It has a limited capacity — typically around seven items — and information fades quickly if not rehearsed. Expert performers use short-term memory efficiently, chunking complex patterns into single meaningful units (“their right winger always cuts inside on the overlap”). Long-term memory, by contrast, is vast and essentially permanent. It stores all the movement patterns, tactics and sport knowledge the performer has ever learned. When a basketball player recognises a defensive formation they have practised against hundreds of times, they retrieve the appropriate offensive response directly from long-term memory — faster than conscious deliberation would allow. This is why experienced players appear to have “more time” on the ball: their long-term memory does the anticipatory work that novices must do consciously and slowly.

Hick’s Law states that reaction time increases with the number of possible responses available. A tennis player who has only one shot in their repertoire decides quickly but predictably. A player with many options takes slightly longer but is much harder to read. This explains why coaches teach multiple responses to the same situation — variety reduces predictability — but must also develop rapid decision making to avoid hesitation. In closed skills with a single correct response (e.g. a swimming start), decision making time is minimal. In open, high-complexity situations (e.g. a football midfielder with multiple passing options), the decision making stage is the critical bottleneck.

Stage 3 — Output

Once a decision is made, the brain transmits output to the muscles via the motor system. The selected movement pattern — retrieved from long-term memory as a motor programme — is sent to the relevant muscle groups to execute the response. For a highly practised skill, this output is rapid and automatic: Adam Peaty’s breaststroke leg kick happens without conscious muscular instruction. For a beginner attempting the same movement, each element must be consciously directed, slowing output considerably. The quality of output depends on both the accuracy of the decision and the technical competence of the performer: even a correct decision can result in poor output if the physical skill is not yet well-learned.

Stage 4 — Feedback

After the movement, the performer receives feedback that feeds back into the input stage, completing the cycle. Feedback can come from internal or external sources. Intrinsic feedback comes from within the performer — the proprioceptive “feel” of a well-struck golf ball, the kinaesthetic sense that a landing was balanced, the physical sensation of muscle fatigue. It is available immediately and continuously during performance. Extrinsic feedback comes from outside — a coach shouting “head up when you pass”, seeing the ball hit the target, reading a score or split time. Extrinsic feedback is particularly important for beginners, who have not yet developed the proprioceptive sensitivity to rely on intrinsic feedback alone. Feedback can also be categorised as knowledge of results (what happened — the ball went in the net) or knowledge of performance (how it was done — the angle of the foot at contact was correct). Knowledge of performance is generally more useful for skill development because it tells the performer specifically what to adjust.

Key Fact

Feedback is the fourth stage of the information processing model and loops back to improve future input. Beginners rely heavily on extrinsic feedback (from coaches) because they lack the body awareness to interpret intrinsic feedback accurately. Elite performers develop rich intrinsic feedback through thousands of repetitions — allowing real-time self-correction without needing coach intervention.

Input: The batsman’s eyes detect the bowler’s run-up, release point, ball trajectory and seam position. Selective attention filters out crowd noise and focuses on early ball flight cues.

Decision making: Short-term memory holds the current pitch conditions and recent deliveries; long-term memory retrieves the movement patterns associated with an outswinger delivery. A decision is made to play a defensive push.

Output: The motor programme for a front-foot defensive stroke is activated. Leg movement, bat angle, head position and weight transfer are all co-ordinated and executed in milliseconds.

Feedback: Intrinsic feedback tells the batsman the shot felt solid and correctly timed. Extrinsic feedback from the coach confirms the head was still, which is knowledge of performance.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘analyse’ questions about information processing, the most common error is listing the four stages without developing how they apply to the sporting scenario in the question. Each stage must be linked to the specific sport context: for example, if the question describes a netball player, your answer should say what they see (input), what they retrieve from memory (decision making), what movement they produce (output) and what they sense or hear after the action (feedback). On 2-mark define questions, always give the core function of the stage, not just its name: ‘short-term memory is a limited-capacity temporary store’ earns more than ‘it stores things for a short time’. For selective attention: always specify that it involves filtering out irrelevant information, not just ‘focusing on the ball’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The information processing model has four stages: input (gathering sensory information from the display, filtered by selective attention), decision making (selecting a response using short-term and long-term memory), output (muscles execute the movement) and feedback (information about the outcome loops back to improve future input).
  • Short-term memory has limited capacity and holds current situational information; long-term memory is vast and permanent, storing all learned movement patterns and tactical knowledge.
  • Beginners rely more on extrinsic feedback and conscious decision making; elite performers use intrinsic feedback and automatic long-term memory retrieval, which is why they appear to have more time and make better decisions under pressure.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the information processing model can explain differences between beginner and elite performers in a fast-paced sport such as basketball.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least three stages of the model clearly distinguishing beginner from elite behaviour at each stage, with specific sporting context throughout. May include: Input/selective attention — beginners struggle to filter the display and attend to irrelevant cues (the ball only) rather than teammates' runs; elite players scan the full court and rapidly attend to significant cues like an opponent's defensive position shifting. Decision making — beginners rely on conscious deliberation and have shallow long-term memory (few stored patterns), making decisions slow and often incorrect; elites retrieve complex tactical patterns instantly from extensive long-term memory, appearing to have more time. Output — beginners produce inconsistent output because the motor programme is poorly established; elites execute fluid, automatic movements. Feedback — beginners depend on extrinsic feedback from coaches because intrinsic proprioceptive feedback is not yet calibrated; elites self-correct in real time using intrinsic feel. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure: Three stages addressed with accurate distinctions and some sporting context. May be less precise on one stage.

Developing: Two stages addressed; distinction between beginner and elite present but underdeveloped; limited sporting context.

Emerging: Stages named but not developed; little or no beginner/elite distinction.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old goalkeeper is learning to face penalty kicks. In training, she faces 20 penalties per session. Evaluate whether improving the input and decision making stages of information processing is more important than improving her output stage for reducing goals conceded.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, consistently applied to the goalkeeper scenario, with a justified conclusion. Arguments that input/decision making matters more: a goalkeeper who cannot read the penalty taker's body language and ball placement cues (input failure) will dive the wrong way regardless of how athletic her dive is; improving selective attention — scanning the run-up angle, non-kicking foot position and hips — could allow her to predict ball direction before contact, narrowing the decision to two or three options; long-term memory stores patterns of penalty takers' preferred side, giving experienced keepers a significant edge at the decision making stage; elite goalkeepers make save decisions largely in the input and decision-making stage — by the time the ball is struck, output is largely reactive. Arguments that output matters more: even correct anticipation is wasted if the diving technique is slow, mistimed or lacking reach; explosive leg drive (output quality) allows the goalkeeper to cover more of the goal even with a less precise prediction; at top speed, the reaction time window means input and decision making have minimal time — output athleticism becomes the decisive factor. Justified conclusion: both stages are interdependent; at beginner level, improving input quality (reading cues) may yield the bigger gain, but output athleticism limits the ceiling of what input improvement can achieve.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the goalkeeper scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development or thin sporting application; may be one-sided.

Emerging: Basic response with little development; may describe stages rather than evaluate them.

lessons.title: Guidance for Beginners and Elite Performers
lessons.description: Visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance and when each is most effective in sport.
lessons.content_html:
Guidance and Feedback — Two Sides of Teaching Sport

Every sports coach has to answer two questions: how do I help the performer learn a skill? And how do I tell them how well they are doing it? The first question is about guidance — the instruction side of coaching. The second is about feedback — the evaluative side. Both are essential, but the most effective type of guidance or feedback varies depending on whether the performer is a beginner or an elite athlete. This lesson focuses on guidance; the types of feedback overlap closely (visual, verbal, intrinsic, extrinsic) and are explored in the same context.

Types of Guidance

There are four types of guidance: visual, verbal, manual and mechanical. Each provides information to the performer through a different sense or medium, and each is more or less suitable depending on the stage of learning.

1. Visual Guidance

Visual guidance is any form of instruction that the performer sees. The most common form is a demonstration: a coach or skilled model performs the skill, and the learner watches and forms a mental image of the correct movement. Beth Mead demonstrating cutting runs in the penalty area to a group of youth players, or a gymnastics coach showing the correct arm position before a balance — these are examples of visual guidance. Video analysis, diagrams of movement paths and highlighted zones on a pitch are also forms of visual guidance.

Visual guidance is highly effective for beginners because it gives a complete picture of what the skill should look like. Beginners have no stored movement pattern in long-term memory to draw on, so seeing the whole skill demonstrated provides the mental blueprint they need. It is also effective for elite performers when combined with video analysis: a sprinter watching slow-motion footage of their arm action, or a swimmer studying their underwater stroke from a poolside camera, can identify technical flaws that verbal description alone would miss. The key limitation is that a demonstration must be accurate — a poor-quality model confuses rather than clarifies.

2. Verbal Guidance

Verbal guidance uses words to instruct. A coach saying “bend your knees on the take-off”, calling “left foot forward” during a defensive drill, or giving tactical instructions before a match are all verbal guidance. Words can convey precise technical information, tactics and corrections quickly. Verbal guidance is extremely time-efficient and can reach a group of performers simultaneously.

However, verbal guidance has limitations for beginners. Complex movements — a butterfly stroke, a javelin release, a cricket drive — are difficult to describe in words alone. A beginner listening to a long verbal explanation of a tennis serve may struggle to translate words into coordinated movement without also seeing it. Verbal guidance works better for performers who already have a movement pattern stored in memory, because the words can activate and refine an existing mental representation. For elite performers, precise verbal cues (“drop the elbow earlier on the catch”) are highly effective because they already understand the movement context and can translate a single cue into a physical adjustment.

Verbal guidance relies on the performer having a mental model to attach the words to. When a coach says “rotate your hips earlier in the swing”, an experienced golfer immediately knows what this means and can adjust. A beginner who has never performed a golf swing has no stored movement pattern, so the instruction is essentially meaningless until they have experienced the physical sensation of the movement. This is why coaches typically combine verbal guidance with visual demonstrations, especially with beginners. The combination — see it, hear it, try it — is far more effective than words alone.

3. Manual Guidance

Manual guidance involves the coach physically moving or supporting the performer. A gymnastics coach manually guiding a child’s arms through a cartwheel, a swimming instructor supporting a learner’s hips at the water surface, or a judo coach physically positioning a student’s stance are all forms of manual guidance. By moving the performer through the correct pattern, the coach gives them a kinaesthetic “feel” for the movement that words and demonstrations cannot fully convey.

Manual guidance is particularly valuable for beginners learning a dangerous or technically complex skill. In gymnastics, manual guidance allows safe learning of skills that could cause injury if performed incorrectly — the coach’s hands on the hips during a round-off build the correct feel without the risk of falling. The main limitation is that over-reliance on manual guidance can create a dependency: the performer learns to rely on the physical support and struggles to replicate the movement independently. Coaches therefore phase it out progressively as the learner internalises the pattern. For elite performers, manual guidance is rarely used because they have established, well-grooved movement patterns; the physical input would more likely disrupt than improve their performance.

4. Mechanical Guidance

Mechanical guidance uses physical aids to support or constrain the movement. Swimming armbands keeping a learner buoyant, a harness and pulley system supporting a diver performing a new somersault, a resistance band guiding arm position in a backstroke drill, or a football target practice goal with reduced netting area are all mechanical guidance devices. Like manual guidance, mechanical guidance provides the performer with a physical sensation of the correct movement and removes the risk of injury during the learning phase.

Mechanical guidance is particularly useful when the consequences of an incorrectly performed skill are dangerous. A gymnast attempting a back somersault for the first time in a safety harness can experience the correct rotation without the risk of a head or neck injury. The limitations mirror those of manual guidance: dependency is a risk. If a swimmer becomes reliant on armbands, they do not develop true water confidence or correct buoyancy control. Mechanical aids should be faded out as competence grows. Elite performers rarely use mechanical guidance for their main sport skill, though they may use specialist equipment such as ergometers or resistance machines for specific conditioning drills.

Key Fact

For beginners: visual guidance (demonstration) and manual guidance (physical support) are most effective — they provide a model and a physical feel for the skill. For elite performers: visual guidance (video analysis) and verbal guidance (precise technical cues) are most appropriate — elites can translate specific words into fine adjustments that would be unnecessary or disruptive to demonstrate physically.

Key Fact

Over-reliance on manual or mechanical guidance can create dependency: the performer can only replicate the skill when physically supported. Coaches should phase out physical aids progressively — increasing independence is the goal, not permanent support. Safety is the main reason for using manual and mechanical guidance with beginners, not long-term skill development.

Guidance and feedback overlap in practice. A demonstration before a skill is visual guidance; a video review after the skill is visual feedback. A coach’s verbal correction during a drill is verbal guidance; a verbal summary at the end of a match is verbal feedback. When evaluating each type, you should be able to justify your choice for a specific performer type, pointing to the performer’s stage of learning, the nature of the skill (open/closed, gross/fine) and any safety considerations.

Feedback types to know alongside guidance: positive feedback reinforces correct technique; negative feedback identifies errors to correct. Knowledge of results tells the performer what happened (the ball went wide); knowledge of performance tells them how they did it (the wrist was too open at contact). Beginners benefit from simple, immediate positive feedback to build confidence; elite performers can handle more detailed, technical, negative feedback to refine near-perfect technique.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On 6-mark analyse questions about guidance, the most effective structure is to: name the guidance type, explain its key feature, then link it specifically to either a beginner or elite performer with a sporting example — and crucially, justify why it suits that performer level. A common error is saying “visual guidance is good for beginners” without explaining why (beginners have no stored movement pattern to refine, so seeing the skill modelled provides the mental blueprint they need). For the 4-mark explain question, always address both the advantage of the guidance type and one limitation. On any question asking you to choose guidance for a specific scenario, read carefully whether the performer is a beginner or elite — the answer is different in each case and the examiner will credit the justification, not just the type named.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four guidance types are: visual (seeing — demonstrations or video), verbal (hearing — spoken or written cues), manual (physical assistance from a coach) and mechanical (equipment or aids constraining or supporting movement).
  • Beginners benefit most from visual and manual guidance — they need a model to copy and a physical feel for the movement. Over-reliance on manual and mechanical guidance creates dependency and should be phased out progressively.
  • Elite performers benefit most from precise verbal guidance and video-based visual feedback, because they can translate technical cues into physical adjustments using their well-developed long-term movement memory.

Up to 2 marks for explaining the limitation for a beginner: the beginner has no stored movement programme in long-term memory (1); they cannot translate abstract verbal instructions into coordinated physical movement without first experiencing or seeing the skill, so verbal guidance alone provides insufficient information to perform the skill (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level athletics coach is deciding which types of guidance to use with two performers: a Year-7 beginner learning the shot-put for the first time, and a county-level sixth-form athlete preparing for a regional competition. Analyse how the coach should use guidance differently for each performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least three guidance types across the two performers, with clear justifications rooted in stage of learning and sporting context. Consistently distinguishes between the two performers throughout. May include: Visual guidance — for the beginner, a full demonstration of the correct put action provides a mental model they have no experience of; for the elite athlete, video analysis of their release angle can reveal subtle technical faults. Verbal guidance — limited use for the beginner because they lack an existing movement programme to attach cues to; highly effective for the elite athlete who can translate a brief cue ('extend the glide phase') into a physical adjustment. Manual guidance — appropriate for the beginner to give the correct kinaesthetic feel for the stance and wrist position; inappropriate for the elite athlete as it disrupts their automatic motor programme. Mechanical guidance — beginners may use a lighter shot or a target circle marked on the ground to constrain practice conditions safely; elite athletes rarely need mechanical guidance. Evaluates the balance rather than listing.

Secure: Three guidance types discussed with mostly accurate justification. Distinguishes between performers on at least two types.

Developing: Two guidance types with some justification; may be less clear on why the difference exists between beginner and elite.

Emerging: One or two types named with little justification; may not distinguish between performers.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club trampolinist is learning a new double somersault. Her coach uses a safety harness during initial practice sessions. Evaluate whether mechanical guidance is always the most appropriate form of guidance when teaching new acrobatic skills, referring to both its benefits and limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, consistently applied to the trampolinist scenario and/or other acrobatic sporting examples, with a justified conclusion. Arguments in support of mechanical guidance: the safety harness allows the athlete to experience the correct rotation of a double somersault without risk of injury; the physical sensation (kinaesthetic feel) from being supported through the skill provides information about the required body position that verbal description could not convey; it builds confidence in a dangerous skill so the performer is not held back by fear; mechanical guidance reduces the risk of reinforcing incorrect patterns by preventing unsafe improvisations. Arguments against / limitations: over-reliance on the harness creates dependency; the trampolinist may fail to develop the internal body control and timing needed to perform unsupported; the harness may alter the feel of the skill slightly, meaning the athlete must still adjust when performing without it; other guidance types may be more appropriate in combination, such as verbal cues ('tuck tighter') and video analysis of existing attempts; for skills with lower danger levels, manual or visual guidance may be equally effective without the dependency risk. Justified conclusion: mechanical guidance is most justified in high-risk acrobatic skills during the early learning phase, but should be progressively withdrawn as competence develops, and combined with verbal and visual guidance for complete skill acquisition.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the sporting scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but underdeveloped; sporting context present but thin or one-sided.

Emerging: Basic response; may list guidance types without evaluating mechanical guidance specifically.

Why Feedback Matters in Sport

Every time a gymnast sticks a landing, a coach calls a correction, or a tennis player hears the crowd react to a shot, information is flowing. That information — feedback — is at the heart of how athletes learn, refine skills and progress. Without it, performers would repeat errors indefinitely. With the right type of feedback, delivered at the right moment, improvement accelerates.

The specification organises feedback into three overlapping categories: its emotional tone (positive or negative), its source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). A single piece of feedback can belong to more than one category simultaneously — for instance, a coach saying “that was an excellent drive, but your follow-through was cut short” is extrinsic, partly positive, partly negative, and contains knowledge of performance.

Positive and Negative Feedback

Positive feedback confirms that an action was performed correctly. It reinforces the movement pattern in the performer’s memory, making it more likely to be repeated. A coach saying “great shoulder rotation on that serve” or a crowd applauding a clean strike are both positive feedback. For beginners especially, positive feedback is powerful — it builds confidence and keeps motivation high at a stage when errors are frequent and self-belief is fragile.

Negative feedback highlights what went wrong and, ideally, what should be done differently. The term “negative” does not mean unkind or demoralising — it simply means the feedback signals a mismatch between what was intended and what was produced. A rugby coach who tells a player “your tackling angle is too narrow, step out wider next time” is giving negative feedback that is precise and constructive. Elite performers often seek and welcome negative feedback because they are confident enough to use it as a tool rather than a threat.

Key Fact

Positive feedback is especially important for beginners because it builds confidence and reinforces correct movements. Negative feedback becomes more valuable for elite performers, who need precise detail on how to refine already high-level technique.

Intrinsic and Extrinsic Feedback

Intrinsic feedback (also called internal feedback) comes from the performer’s own body. It travels through sensory channels: proprioception (the sense of where your limbs are in space), vision, touch and hearing. A gymnast knows her balance beam routine felt fluent because her proprioceptive system reports smooth weight transfer and correctly timed muscle contractions. A cricketer senses from the impact vibration through the bat handle whether the ball was struck from the middle of the bat. Intrinsic feedback is instantaneous and continuous — it arrives during and immediately after every movement.

For intrinsic feedback to be useful, the performer must have the experience and body awareness to interpret the sensations correctly. Beginners often struggle to do this — they may feel that a movement went well when it did not, because they lack the kinaesthetic reference point of what “correct” feels like. Elite athletes, by contrast, are highly attuned to intrinsic feedback: Mo Farah described being able to sense the precise moment his running economy started to drop in the final 200 m of a 5,000 m race.

Extrinsic feedback (external feedback) originates outside the performer. Sources include coaches and teachers, peers, video analysis, heart rate monitors, scoreboards and the crowd. Because it comes from outside, extrinsic feedback can fill the gaps that intrinsic feedback misses — for example, a sprinter cannot feel the exact angle of her block start, but her coach can see it on a camera and give precise corrections.

A common error is assuming that because intrinsic feedback is immediate, it must be accurate. Beginners lack the kinaesthetic memory to judge “correct” feeling — a novice swimmer may feel that her arm entry is clean when it is actually crossed over the midline. This is precisely why extrinsic feedback from a coach or video is so critical in early learning: it provides a reliable external reference point until the performer builds a more accurate internal model.

Knowledge of Results and Knowledge of Performance

Knowledge of results (KR) tells the performer what the outcome was: the shot went wide, the javelin landed at 42 metres, the race was completed in 13.8 seconds. It is always extrinsic because the result is separate from the movement itself. KR is easy to understand and motivating — seeing a time improve from 14.2 s to 13.8 s gives a clear signal that training is working — but it tells the performer nothing about why the result was what it was, or how to change it.

Knowledge of performance (KP) focuses on the quality of the movement: the hips rotated too early, the release angle was too flat, the elbow position was correct. KP is richer than KR and more directly actionable because it tells the performer what to change. A coach watching a discus thrower and saying “your pivot foot twisted before your non-throwing arm swept across — you lost rotation” is giving knowledge of performance. Elite performers typically benefit more from KP because their outcomes are already competitive and fine technical detail is what separates them from rivals.

Key Fact

Knowledge of results (KR) = the outcome (time, score, distance). Knowledge of performance (KP) = the quality of the technique. KR motivates; KP teaches. Elite performers need both, but KP is the more powerful learning tool.

Choosing the Right Feedback for the Performer

The effectiveness of feedback depends on the performer’s stage of learning. Beginners benefit most from positive feedback (to build confidence), extrinsic feedback (because intrinsic awareness is unreliable), and knowledge of results (which is simple to understand). Overloading a beginner with detailed KP can cause confusion and undermine motivation.

Elite performers, on the other hand, respond best to specific negative and positive feedback on technique (KP), as well as their own well-developed intrinsic feedback. They also benefit from extrinsic sources such as video analysis and data from performance monitoring equipment. The key principle is that feedback should always be actionable — vague comments such as “try harder” or “that was good” without further detail have little learning value regardless of the performer’s level.

In the basic information processing model you studied in the previous lesson, feedback is the final stage that loops back into the input. Intrinsic feedback feeds into the system through the sensory display (sight, touch, proprioception). Extrinsic feedback arrives as a new input — the coach’s voice or the video replay enters the input stage alongside environmental information from the display. Both types then influence decision making in the next attempt, helping the performer select a more appropriate motor response from long-term memory. This loop is why consistent, timely feedback speeds up skill acquisition.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 2 marks — Define question, you need a precise one-sentence definition. “Positive feedback is good feedback” earns nothing — you must specify what it does (reinforces correct actions) and when it is most effective (for beginners). For a 4 marks — Explain question, give the definition (1 mark), explain the mechanism (1 mark), add the sporting example (1 mark), then link to the level of performer (1 mark). A very common error on feedback questions is confusing intrinsic/extrinsic (the source) with positive/negative (the tone) — these are separate dimensions and should never be swapped. On a 6 marks — Analyse question about feedback types, avoid bullet-pointing: instead write a developed paragraph that states a feedback type, explains what it does, applies it to a sporting context and evaluates its strengths and limitations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Feedback has three dimensions: emotional tone (positive or negative), source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). These categories overlap — a single piece of feedback can fit all three simultaneously.
  • Beginners benefit most from positive, extrinsic feedback and simple knowledge of results; elite performers gain more from specific, technique-focused knowledge of performance and their own well-developed intrinsic feedback.
  • Feedback must be actionable to have learning value — vague praise or criticism does not help performers identify what to change or repeat.

lessons.title: Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory
lessons.description: How arousal affects sporting performance and the stress management techniques athletes use.
lessons.content_html:
What is Arousal?

Arousal is the level of activation or readiness in the mind and body. It sits on a continuous spectrum — from deep sleep at one extreme, through calm alertness, to intense excitement and panic at the other. In sport, arousal is neither simply “nervousness” nor simply “motivation” — it is the physiological and psychological state that underpins how prepared a performer is to act. Heart rate rises, muscles become primed, attention sharpens or narrows. Whether those changes help or hinder performance depends on whether arousal is at the right level for the task.

Two key factors determine the optimal level of arousal for a task: the type of skill involved, and the performer’s experience. A rugby flanker driving into a tackle needs high arousal — the task is physically explosive, relies on gross motor patterns and benefits from heightened aggression. A snooker player lining up a final-frame deciding shot needs low arousal — fine motor control, precision and concentration demand calm. Gross skills tolerate and often benefit from high arousal; fine skills require low arousal to execute precisely.

The Inverted-U Theory

The inverted-U theory describes the relationship between arousal and performance using a characteristic curve. Imagine a graph with arousal level on the x-axis (running left to right from low to high) and performance level on the y-axis (running bottom to top from low to high). The resulting curve rises as arousal increases from zero, reaches a single peak at the point of optimal arousal, then falls symmetrically as arousal continues to climb beyond that peak.

The theory has three zones. In the under-arousal zone (left of the peak), the performer is insufficiently activated: concentration is poor, reactions are slow and motivation is absent. A footballer who is mentally “switched off” before a routine match may misplace simple passes they would never usually get wrong. In the optimal arousal zone (the peak), the performer is precisely prepared — alert, focused and physically primed. In the over-arousal zone (right of the peak), excessive nervousness or excitement floods the system: decision making deteriorates, fine motor control breaks down, and anxiety may cause “choking”. Dina Asher-Smith has spoken candidly about managing the risk of over-arousal before major sprint finals, using controlled breathing and mental routines to stay on the peak rather than tipping over it.

Key Fact

On the inverted-U graph: x-axis = arousal level (low to high), y-axis = performance level (low to high). The peak is ‘optimal arousal’. Left of the peak = under-arousal, performance is low. Right of the peak = over-arousal, performance is also low. The skill type determines where the peak sits: gross skills peak further right (higher arousal needed); fine skills peak further left (lower arousal needed).

Linking Arousal Level to Skill Type

The inverted-U curve does not sit in the same position for every skill. A 100 m sprinter’s optimal arousal point sits towards the higher end of the arousal axis — the explosive, gross motor demands of sprinting are enhanced by a surge in adrenaline, elevated heart rate and heightened muscular tension. But the optimal arousal level for a golfer executing a delicate chip shot from the fringe of a green sits much further left. The precise wrist action, measured swing speed and judged clubface angle all require fine motor control that falls apart under excess activation.

As a rule: gross skills benefit from higher arousal. A tackle in rugby, a power lift in weightlifting, a full-force drive in shot put — all benefit from the extra tension and activation that high arousal brings. Fine skills require lower arousal. Archery, snooker, ten-pin bowling, the free throw in basketball, a conversion kick in rugby — all demand the calm, controlled motor programme execution that high arousal disrupts. This is why a basketball player who is highly aroused may dominate a physical post-up battle but then miss the free throws awarded when they are fouled.

Students often assume the inverted-U peak is in a fixed position for everyone performing the same sport. In reality, the optimal arousal point varies between individuals as well as between skills. A highly experienced athlete who competes regularly at elite level may have a higher optimal arousal threshold — they’ve built the mental skills to channel arousal into performance. A beginner in the same sport may over-arouse much sooner. Additionally, personality influences the threshold: extroverts generally require more stimulation (higher arousal) to reach their optimal point, while introverts can peak at a lower level of activation. The theory is best applied as a guide for the individual performer and the specific skill, not as a universal rule for an entire sport.

Stress Management Techniques

When a performer’s arousal is too high — particularly in high-stakes competition — they need practical tools to bring it back towards optimal. The specification identifies three key techniques: deep breathing, mental rehearsal (visualisation/imagery) and positive self-talk.

Deep breathing works by activating the parasympathetic nervous system, which counteracts the fight-or-flight response of over-arousal. The technique involves inhaling slowly through the nose for a count of four, holding briefly, then exhaling slowly through the mouth for a count of six or eight. The extended exhalation is the physiologically critical part — it drives down heart rate and signals to the brain that the threat level is low. A rugby kicker using deep breathing before a pressure conversion is not wasting time — they are chemically resetting their nervous system. It is used before free throws, set pieces, serves and any moment when a task-specific motor programme must be executed cleanly.

Mental rehearsal — also known as visualisation or imagery — involves the performer building a detailed mental simulation of their performance before it happens. Research shows that vividly imagined movement activates many of the same neural pathways as actually performing it. Adam Peaty has described using detailed visualisation of his 100 m breaststroke race before every major competition, including the sensation of water resistance, the rhythm of his pull, and the moment of turning at the wall. Effective mental rehearsal uses all senses and is always performed in the first person, from the performer’s own perspective, picturing success rather than failure.

Positive self-talk involves consciously replacing negative internal dialogue with pre-planned affirming statements. Athletes under pressure are prone to catastrophic thinking (“I always miss these”, “everyone is watching me fail”). Positive self-talk interrupts this loop: the performer has a prepared phrase — “I have trained for this”, “smooth and accurate”, “trust the process” — that redirects attention onto the task cues rather than the feared outcome. It reduces cognitive anxiety without requiring a physiological reset, making it the quickest of the three techniques to deploy mid-performance.

Key Fact

Three AQA stress management techniques: (1) Deep breathing — slows breathing and heart rate, calms the nervous system, used before or during performance. (2) Mental rehearsal / visualisation / imagery — creates a vivid mental simulation of successful performance, activating the same neural pathways as physical practice. (3) Positive self-talk — replaces negative thoughts with affirming statements to refocus attention and maintain confidence.

Coaches also deal with the opposite problem: athletes who arrive at competition insufficiently aroused, perhaps because the event feels routine or because they are physically fatigued. Under-arousal produces slow reactions, poor concentration, reduced effort and sloppy decision making. Techniques to increase arousal include energetic music, team talks that raise emotional intensity, fast-paced warm-up drills and the coach deliberately raising the perceived stakes of the competition. ‘Psyching up’ strategies are the mirror image of the calming techniques above — the goal is always to land the performer at their personal optimal point on the inverted-U.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 2 marks — Define question on arousal, you must include both the physical and mental dimension — “a state of physical and mental readiness/activation”. Saying only “being nervous” or “being motivated” earns nothing because it’s too vague. For the inverted-U graph question (“draw and label”), examiners require: a correctly shaped curve, labelled x-axis (arousal level), labelled y-axis (performance level), and the peak labelled ‘optimal arousal’ or equivalent. Unlabelled axes score zero for the labelling marks. On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about arousal and performance, students frequently produce one-sided answers listing only ways arousal helps. Full marks require both the positive effects of optimal arousal and the negative effects of over- or under-arousal, with a sporting example for each point and a balanced conclusion. Structure each paragraph as ‘For… because… for example… However…’ to ensure you cover both sides systematically.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Arousal is the level of physical and mental activation in a performer. The inverted-U theory shows that performance is best at an optimal arousal level — too little causes under-performance through lethargy; too much causes over-performance through anxiety and loss of fine motor control.
  • Optimal arousal varies by skill type: gross skills (tackling, sprinting, throwing) require higher arousal; fine skills (archery, snooker, a penalty kick) require lower arousal to preserve motor precision.
  • Three stress management techniques lower over-arousal: deep breathing (slows heart rate via the parasympathetic system), mental rehearsal/visualisation (simulates successful performance), and positive self-talk (replaces negative thoughts with affirming cues).
