lessons.title: Sedentary Lifestyle, Obesity and Somatotypes
lessons.description: Consequences of inactivity, how obesity affects performance, and ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph body types.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Sedentary Lifestyle?

A sedentary lifestyle is one defined by prolonged physical inactivity. The word “sedentary” comes from the Latin for “sitting”, and that is its defining feature: large portions of waking hours spent sitting or lying down, with minimal structured exercise. Modern technology has made sedentary living increasingly easy — screen-based entertainment, desk-based work and motorised transport can combine to mean that some individuals complete fewer than 2,000 steps a day.

The consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are cumulative and wide-ranging. They span physical health (weight gain, disease), mental health (depression, low self-esteem) and social health (isolation, withdrawal). Understanding these consequences as distinct but interconnected categories is important for exam answers and for appreciating why public health campaigns consistently promote active living.

Key Fact

The seven consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are: weight gain/obesity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, poor sleep, poor self-esteem and lethargy. Obesity itself then creates a secondary cascade of health consequences.

Consequences of a Sedentary Lifestyle

Weight gain and obesity: without regular physical activity to burn calories, energy intake consistently exceeds energy expenditure. The surplus energy is stored as body fat. Over time, this leads to excess body weight and, if severe, to obesity. Unused saturated fat also accumulates in the blood vessels, contributing to the narrowing and hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis) that underlies much cardiovascular disease.

Heart disease and hypertension: a sedentary heart is a weaker, less efficient heart. Without the regular challenge of aerobic exercise, the heart muscle does not strengthen, cardiac output does not improve and blood vessels lose some of their elasticity. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is strongly associated with physical inactivity and is a major risk factor for heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease. A sedentary lifestyle is one of the most modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

Diabetes: physical inactivity reduces the body’s sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose. When cells become resistant to insulin, blood glucose rises. Over time this can develop into type 2 diabetes, which carries serious long-term complications including nerve damage, vision loss and cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity, which is why increased physical activity is a first-line recommendation for individuals at risk.

Poor sleep and lethargy: regular exercise improves sleep quality by regulating circadian rhythms and reducing anxiety. A sedentary individual who does not exercise regularly may find it harder to fall asleep and experience less restorative deep sleep. Poor sleep in turn causes lethargy — persistent tiredness and a lack of energy — which makes further activity feel even less appealing, reinforcing the sedentary cycle.

Poor self-esteem: physical inactivity is associated with reduced self-efficacy, weight gain and social withdrawal. Self-esteem — one’s sense of personal worth — is strongly linked to physical self-perception. Individuals who are inactive and overweight often report lower confidence in their bodies and in social situations. This can contribute to depression and further withdrawal from activity, completing a damaging cycle.

Obesity: Definition and Impact on Performance

Obesity is defined medically as an excess accumulation of body fat sufficient to adversely affect health, typically measured by a body mass index (BMI) over 30. For a GCSE student, the key point is that obesity is not simply a cosmetic concern — it has direct, measurable impacts on a person’s ability to perform in physical activity and sport.

Limits cardiovascular endurance: excess body mass increases the oxygen demand on the cardiovascular system during exercise. The heart must work harder to pump blood to a larger body, and the lungs must work harder to supply sufficient oxygen. This means an obese individual reaches their maximum heart rate at lower exercise intensities, runs out of breath sooner and fatigues faster. Stamina (cardiovascular endurance) is significantly impaired.

Limits flexibility: excess fat tissue around joints and the abdomen physically restricts the range of movement at key joints. An obese individual will typically have a reduced ability to flex at the hip, extend the spine and perform movements requiring full range of motion. This makes activities such as gymnastics, martial arts and any sport demanding joint mobility significantly harder.

Limits agility: agility — the ability to change direction quickly and accurately — requires low body mass relative to muscle strength. Excess body fat increases the load that the muscles and joints must move during direction changes, reducing agility and increasing injury risk (particularly to the knees and ankles).

Limits speed and power: speed depends on the ratio of muscular force to body mass. An obese individual carries more mass that must be accelerated by their muscles, directly reducing stride frequency, acceleration and maximum speed. Power output (force × velocity) is similarly compromised when body mass is excessive relative to muscle mass.

Students sometimes confuse being overweight with being obese, or assume that all excess mass is automatically a disadvantage. This is an oversimplification. A professional rugby prop or heavyweight boxer may have a high BMI because of their large muscle mass — they are not medically obese, and their body composition suits their sport. The spec’s discussion of obesity specifically refers to excess body fat, not body mass in general. When evaluating somatotypes and body composition in sport, distinguish between lean body mass (muscle, bone) and fat mass — it is the proportion of fat mass that determines whether obesity is a limiting factor.

Somatotypes: Body Type in Sport

The concept of somatotype was developed in the 1940s by psychologist William Sheldon, who identified three idealised body types. In GCSE PE, somatotypes are used to discuss the relationship between body shape and sporting suitability. Most real people are a blend of all three types, but understanding the extremes is useful for sports science analysis.

The endomorph has a pear-shaped body characterised by wide hips, a high percentage of body fat, relatively narrow shoulders and shorter limbs. Endomorphs tend to have difficulty losing weight but can carry significant muscle mass. In sport, a pure endomorph faces challenges in activities requiring speed, agility and cardiovascular endurance. However, in contact sports where body mass is an advantage (sumo wrestling, certain positions in American football), an endomorphic body type can be beneficial.

The mesomorph is widely regarded as the most versatile sporting body type. Mesomorphs have wide shoulders, a narrow waist, well-defined musculature and a naturally low body fat percentage. They respond quickly to training and gain muscle easily. This body type suits a wide range of sports, including sprinting, gymnastics, swimming and team sports. Athletes like Usain Bolt and Dame Sarah Storey exhibit mesomorphic characteristics, though both also show elements of other somatotypes.

The ectomorph is long, lean and lightly muscled. Ectomorphs have narrow hips and shoulders, long limbs and very little body fat. They may struggle to build muscle mass and can be susceptible to the cold. However, long limbs and low body mass make ectomorphs naturally suited to endurance activities (marathon running, long-distance cycling) and sports where height and reach are advantageous (basketball, volleyball). Paula Radcliffe exemplified many ectomorphic traits that suited elite marathon performance.

The spec asks students to “identify the most suitable body type for particular sports (or positions within a sport) and justify their choice”. This means your answer must include three steps: name the somatotype, describe the relevant physical characteristics, and link those characteristics to specific demands of the sport or position.

Example: “A mesomorph is most suited to gymnastics because their wide shoulders support overhead strength, their low body fat enables the strength-to-weight ratio needed for apparatus work, and their well-defined musculature responds quickly to the explosive power demands of floor and vault routines.” Avoid the error of stating only the body type without the justification — most somatotype questions award the majority of marks for the justified link to sport.

Key Fact

Endomorph: pear-shaped, wide hips, high fat — suited to contact sports requiring mass. Mesomorph: muscular, low fat, wide shoulders — versatile, suited to power and team sports. Ectomorph: lean, long limbs, low mass — suited to endurance and height-dependent sports.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 9-mark evaluate questions on sedentary lifestyle and obesity, the most common error is listing consequences without evaluating the severity of each or considering whether any consequences are harder to reverse than others. A Mastering-band answer will distinguish between physical, mental and social consequences; will argue which is most significant (with justification); and will consider a counter-argument (e.g. “while physical consequences such as heart disease are serious, they can be addressed through lifestyle change — however, the mental health consequences such as depression are often harder to treat and self-perpetuating”). For somatotype questions, always name the somatotype, give characteristics and justify the link to sport — a one-word answer (“mesomorph”) without justification will not score the marks available. For 6-mark analyse questions on obesity’s effect on performance, use the four performance components (cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, agility, speed/power) as your structure and develop each one.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A sedentary lifestyle causes seven key consequences: weight gain/obesity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, poor sleep, poor self-esteem and lethargy — affecting physical, mental and social health.
  • Obesity limits sporting performance across four key areas: cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, agility and speed/power — all arising from excess fat mass increasing the load on the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems.
  • The three somatotypes — endomorph (wide hips, high fat), mesomorph (muscular, low fat), ectomorph (lean, long limbs) — each suit different sports, and justifying the link to sporting demands is essential in exam answers.

lessons.title: Energy, Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
lessons.description: Daily energy needs, macronutrients, balanced diet ratios and the effects of dehydration on sport.
lessons.content_html:
Energy: The Fuel for Sport and Life

Everything the body does — breathing, thinking, sprinting, lifting — requires energy. That energy is measured in kilocalories (Kcal) and comes entirely from the food we eat. The average adult male requires approximately 2,500 Kcal per day, while the average adult female requires around 2,000 Kcal per day. However, these are only averages — how much energy any individual actually needs depends on four key factors: age, gender, height, and energy expenditure (how much exercise they do). A 16-year-old county-level swimmer training twice a day will have far greater energy needs than a sedentary adult of the same height and gender.

Key Fact

An individual’s daily energy requirement is affected by age, gender, height, and energy expenditure. Average values are 2,500 Kcal/day for males and 2,000 Kcal/day for females — but athletes and highly active individuals need significantly more.

The Balanced Diet: Proportions and Purposes

A balanced diet does not mean eating equal amounts of everything. It means eating the right proportions of different food types to supply the body with all the nutrients it needs. No single food provides every nutrient — variety is essential. Unused energy, particularly from saturated fats, is stored as body fat, which can contribute to obesity over time. The specification requires you to know the approximate percentage breakdown of a balanced diet: 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, and 15–20% protein. These proportions reflect the primary roles each macronutrient plays in the body.

Macronutrients: Carbohydrate, Fat and Protein

Carbohydrate is the primary and preferred fuel for all types of exercise, regardless of intensity. Whether a performer is jogging at a comfortable pace or sprinting at maximum effort, carbohydrates are the first fuel the body calls upon. They are broken down into glucose, which is either used immediately or stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver for use during exercise. Elite distance runners such as Dina Asher-Smith prepare for competition partly by ensuring glycogen stores are fully loaded through carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before an event.

Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate, but it can only be used efficiently as a fuel source at low intensity — for example, during a slow, steady-state walk or easy cycle ride. When exercise intensity increases, the body switches back to carbohydrate because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the demand. Fat also has important non-energy roles: it insulates the body, protects organs, and is a carrier for fat-soluble vitamins.

Protein is not a primary energy source. Its main role is the growth and repair of muscle tissue — essential after heavy training when muscle fibres have been broken down by the work they have done. Adam Peaty, for example, follows a protein-rich recovery plan after intense pool sessions to support muscle repair and adaptation. Consuming insufficient protein slows recovery and limits the adaptations (such as hypertrophy) that training is designed to produce.

Vitamins and minerals do not supply energy directly, but they are essential for the efficient working of all body systems. Vitamins support processes from immune function to bone health; minerals such as calcium and iron are vital for bone density and oxygen transport in the blood respectively. The specification does not require you to name specific vitamins or minerals, but you should know that their role is to maintain the efficient working of body systems and general health. A diet lacking in variety will typically be deficient in vitamins and minerals even if its Kcal total looks adequate on paper.

Key Fact

A balanced diet is approximately 55–60% carbohydrate (main energy source), 25–30% fat (energy at low intensity; insulation), 15–20% protein (growth and repair). Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities.

Hydration and the Consequences of Dehydration

Water is not just a drink — it is the medium in which almost every chemical reaction in the body takes place. Maintaining water balance (hydration) is critical to performance. Even a 1–2% reduction in body mass through fluid loss can begin to impair sporting performance. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. During intense exercise in warm conditions — such as a cross-country race or a summer football tournament — sweat rates can be high, meaning fluid must be replaced regularly to maintain performance and safety.

Effects of Dehydration on the Body and Performance

Dehydration triggers a series of interconnected physiological problems. As fluid is lost, blood plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker. This increase in blood viscosity means the heart must work harder to push blood around the circulatory system, driving up heart rate. Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles slows, accelerating fatigue. In severe cases, heart rhythm may become irregular. Meanwhile, the body’s ability to shed heat through the blood vessels near the skin is compromised, causing core body temperature to rise — increasing the risk of overheating and heat stroke.

Beyond the cardiovascular effects, dehydration also affects the nervous system. Reaction time slows and decision-making deteriorates — a basketball player who is even mildly dehydrated may make slower, poorer decisions on court. Muscle function degrades too: dehydrated muscles fatigue more rapidly and are more prone to cramping, because the electrolyte balance (sodium, potassium) that enables muscle contraction is disrupted. For a sprint cyclist like Geraint Thomas, any cramping or slowing of reaction time in the final kilometre of a race could be decisive.

A common misconception is that hydration simply means “drink lots.” The spec focuses on balance — maintaining appropriate water levels, not overloading with fluids. The assessment reward is for understanding the cascade of effects from dehydration: thicker blood → higher heart rate → slower delivery of oxygen → muscle fatigue/cramp → slower reactions → poorer decisions. Practise writing that chain in order without notes, anchored to a sporting example.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On “Calculate” and “Calculate from Data” questions involving nutrition, always show your working, state the units (Kcal, %, g) and box your final answer. If asked to calculate the energy from carbohydrate in a diet of 2,400 Kcal, the working is: 2,400 × 0.55 = 1,320 Kcal from carbohydrate (or 2,400 × 0.60 = 1,440 Kcal at the upper end of the range). Missing the unit drops a mark.

On a 6-mark “Analyse” question about dehydration, avoid listing effects without connecting them. Write each effect as a cause-and-effect chain: “Dehydration reduces blood plasma volume, which increases blood viscosity (thickness). The heart must then beat faster to maintain blood flow, leading to earlier fatigue, and reduced oxygen delivery to working muscles.” That single chain earns more credit than five disconnected bullet points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is measured in Kcal. Daily needs (avg. 2,500 Kcal male / 2,000 Kcal female) vary with age, gender, height and exercise levels. A balanced diet is 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, 15–20% protein — carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all intensities.
  • Protein’s role is growth and repair of muscle tissue. Fat provides energy only at low intensity and in larger amounts than carbohydrate per gram. Vitamins and minerals maintain efficient body system function.
  • Dehydration increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate, causes overheating, slows reactions, impairs decision-making and causes muscle fatigue and cramps — all of which degrade sporting performance.

lessons.title: Interpreting Data on Participation and Performance
lessons.description: Read tables, bar charts, line graphs and pie charts about sport, participation and wellbeing.
lessons.content_html:
Why Data Skills Matter in PE

Physical education is not just about sport — it also requires you to make sense of evidence. Data appears across this paper in questions about participation rates, health trends, fitness scores and commercial figures. The ability to read a graph accurately, make a comparison, calculate a percentage change, and then explain what the numbers actually mean in a sporting or wellbeing context is tested directly in questions worth up to four marks. These marks are predictable and highly attainable if you follow a clear method.

Types of Data: Quantitative and Qualitative

Quantitative data deals with numbers. It can be collected through questionnaires (tick-box formats, rating scales) and surveys. Examples in a PE context include the number of students who exercise three or more times a week, a table of body mass index (BMI) values, or a bar chart of participation in different sports by gender.

Qualitative data deals with descriptions, opinions and experiences. It cannot be counted directly. Common collection methods are interviews and structured or unstructured observations. A PE researcher conducting in-depth interviews with teenage girls about barriers to sport participation would be collecting qualitative data. Qualitative data is rich and detailed, but it cannot be placed on a graph in the same way as quantitative figures.

Presenting Data: Tables, Bar Charts, Line Graphs and Pie Charts

Data can be displayed in four main formats, each with strengths for different purposes. A table presents raw values in rows and columns, making exact figures easy to read. A bar chart uses rectangular bars to compare values across categories — for example, comparing weekly participation in different sports. Both axes must be labelled: the horizontal (x) axis typically shows the category (sport, age group, school); the vertical (y) axis shows the value being measured (number of participants, percentage, score).

A line graph is used to show change over time — for example, tracking the average resting heart rate of a cohort over a 12-week fitness programme. Each point on the line represents a value at a specific time, and the trend (rising, falling, levelling off) is the key thing to describe. A pie chart displays proportions as slices of a circle, with each slice representing a percentage or share of the whole. Pie charts are commonly used to show the distribution of media revenue across sports, or the breakdown of a population’s activity levels.

Key Fact

Bar charts compare categories. Line graphs show change over time. Pie charts show proportions. Tables give exact figures. Both axes on bar charts and line graphs must always be labelled with the variable name and its unit.

How to Interpret Data: A Four-Step Method

Examiners reward the inference (what the data means) more than simply reading off a figure. A reliable method for any interpret-data question is: (1) Read — identify the exact values you need from the chart or table. (2) Compare — compare at least two figures (e.g. between two groups, two time points, or two sports). (3) Calculate — if the question asks for it, calculate the difference, percentage share, or percentage change. (4) Explain — state what the comparison means in a sporting or wellbeing context. Missing step 4 is the most common reason students drop marks: copying a number from a table earns nothing if the question asks you to “interpret.”

Imagine a bar chart shows weekly participation in netball at three Year-10 schools: School A 18%, School B 27%, School C 12%. A typical 4-mark question asks: “Interpret what the data shows about participation patterns across the three schools.”

Step 1 (Read): School B has the highest participation at 27%; School C has the lowest at 12%.
Step 2 (Compare): School B’s rate is 15 percentage points higher than School C’s (27 − 12 = 15).
Step 3 (Calculate if needed): School B has more than twice School C’s participation (27 ÷ 12 = 2.25×).
Step 4 (Explain): This suggests significant variation in engagement patterns between schools, which could reflect differences in facilities, media coverage, role models or socio-economic factors in the local area.

Calculating Percentage Change and Mean

Two calculations appear regularly. Percentage change is calculated as: (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. For example, if the number of female participants in a club rises from 40 to 52, the percentage change is (52 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = 30%. The mean (average) is the sum of all values divided by the number of values. The range (highest minus lowest) describes the spread of data. Always state your units (bpm, %, Kcal, participants) and show working for calculation questions.

Key Fact

Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Mean = sum ÷ number of values. Range = highest − lowest. Always show working and include units in your final answer.

A very common error on 4-mark interpret-data questions is simply copying numbers from the table or graph: “School A has 18%, School B has 27%, School C has 12%.” This reads the data but does not interpret it. Mark schemes require: a comparison (quoting at least two figures), a calculated difference or ratio where appropriate, and a sporting or wellbeing explanation for what the pattern suggests. Practise finishing every data answer with the phrase “This suggests that…” and completing the sentence with a real-world implication.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On “Interpret Data” questions (4 marks), never just copy figures — the examiner wants a comparison, a calculation if needed, and an explanation of what the data means in context. Structure your answer as: (1) state the highest and lowest values with their labels; (2) calculate the difference or percentage change; (3) explain the sporting or wellbeing implication. Quote at least two figures from the data and always include units. Students who write “School B is higher” without quoting the value typically earn 1 mark; students who quote values, compare them, and explain the sporting implication earn 3–4 marks.

On “Calculate from Data” questions (3 marks), the mark scheme typically awards 1 mark for correct working, 1 mark for the correct figure, and 1 mark for stating the unit. Show all three steps even if the arithmetic feels straightforward — forgetting the unit after a correct calculation costs a mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Quantitative data uses numbers (collected via questionnaires/surveys); qualitative data uses descriptions (collected via interviews/observations). Bar charts compare categories; line graphs show change over time; pie charts show proportions; tables give exact values. Always label both axes.
  • The four-step interpret method: Read → Compare → Calculate → Explain. Examiners reward the sporting/wellbeing inference, not just reading a number from the chart.
  • Key formulae: percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100; mean = sum ÷ number of values; range = highest − lowest. Always show working and state units (%, bpm, Kcal, participants).

Data that deals with descriptions, opinions and experiences rather than numbers, collected through interviews or observations.

A circular chart divided into slices to show proportions or percentage shares of a whole data set.
